prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, based on magic-wavelength trapping, which brought time and frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I moved B031 to the top of my own list after reading the openings. Three colleagues (Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth) independently reached it as first choice, and their attribution accounts agree with mine. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice in 2001-2003 and made the first demonstrations, which is the original experiment. Ye's group then took it to record accuracy and stability and to many-body clock physics. It is an invention that opens a door: relativistic geodesy, tests of constants, dark-matter searches and a redefinition of the second are all being pursued with it. Many laboratories (Tokyo/RIKEN, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) have verified and surpassed each other at the 10^-18 level, so the result is experimentally verified and mature, with a clean two-name credit that fits the supplied names.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty. Hall and Hansch (2005) were honoured for the frequency comb and Wineland (2012) for ion control, so a sceptic can call lattice clocks an incremental refinement of optical frequency standards. Priority is also not entirely clean: Ludlow, Takamoto, Lemonde and others made decisive early lattice-clock demonstrations that are not credited. Some of the strongest applications, such as the redefinition of the second and geodesy, are still prospective rather than realised. My own first choice, B009, would be the better answer if the committee wanted to prioritise an instrument invention that has already transformed a whole field, but I now weigh its attribution problem too heavily (Krivanek) and its wider support too thin.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B031 first as a clean case of an original idea (magic wavelength) and record-level precision, with a two-person credit, but asks whether it is merely incremental after 2005 and the ion-clock work of 2012.
responses.response: I agree with the credit and with the concern, and I think the answer is in the record. The comb gave a way to count optical cycles. The lattice clock solved a different problem, how to hold a large number of neutral atoms without perturbing the transition, which the 2005 prize did not address and the ion clocks cannot do at the same stability. That is a distinct invention. Still, I would want the citation to name the magic-wavelength trapping idea explicitly so that the prize is not read as a second comb prize.

responses.point: Mehlig placed B031 only eighth, while accepting that the idea is simple and general and the impact clear, and put the twisted bilayer graphene candidate B024 first because the mechanism is understood and was predicted before it was observed.
responses.response: I respect that B024 is a striking and well-reproduced story, and it was my third choice. I would still put it behind B031 for now, since the experimental interpretation is not settled: the origin of the superconductivity remains debated, and the first-author experimentalists (Cao and colleagues) fall outside any three-name credit. I would like Mehlig to say what ranks B031 so low, because his own maturity assessment calls it mature and his attribution assessment calls the pair natural. If it is the novelty question, we should discuss that directly.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the Higgs discovery B005 first as a decisive and overdue experimental result, and puts B009 fourth, noting the Wolf and Kavli recognition of Rose, Haider and Urban.
responses.response: I agree that B005 is a scientific first-rank discovery, and I would not say otherwise. My difficulty is the three-person limit: any trio from Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee leaves out people whose work was equally decisive, and four different colleagues proposed three different trios. For the original-experiment standard I take seriously, I cannot be absolutely sure we have named the right people. B031 does not have that problem. On B009, Pearce is right about Wolf 2011, but the Kavli 2020 prize also included Krivanek, and his absence from the credited names is a real weakness for the committee.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B009 fifth and calls it an overdue instrument advance, but flags that Krivanek and co-workers on the STEM corrector are not in the credited names and that the committee must decide whether an instrument advance is a discovery of physics.
responses.response: I agree with both points, and I raise them against my own opening first choice. On Krivanek, the TEM corrector (Haider, Rose, Urban) and the STEM corrector (Krivanek, Dellby, Batson) were developed in parallel, so the credit cannot be settled by the supplied three names alone. On whether instrumentation counts, the statutes permit an invention, and Ruska in 1986 is a precedent, but the committee should be consistent: B031 is also an instrument, though it comes with a fundamental-physics return. I therefore keep B009 as an alternative rather than my preferred choice.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B031 first and B028 (ultracold atoms in optical lattices, Hubbard model) second, noting that five credited names compete for three places and that the earlier BEC and laser-cooling prizes overlap with it.
responses.response: I agree with her ordering. B028 is an important field, but I find the attribution too unsettled at the moment: Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger, Zoller and Cirac each have a plausible claim, and Jaksch is missing from the list altogether. I would keep it off my configuration for the present, and I would not combine it with B031, since that would exceed the three-person limit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Priority among Katori, Ye, Ludlow, Takamoto, Lemonde and others in the first lattice-clock demonstrations; I rely on memory and cannot verify it from the supplied files.
Whether the Krivanek (STEM corrector) priority question can be resolved for B009 if it is brought forward as the alternative.
A two-part configuration combining B031 with B009 would need five names, so it cannot be offered within the three-person limit without dropping a laureate.
statement.conflict_note: B009 (aberration-corrected electron microscopy) lies directly in my own field of work and in the community I preside over (IFSM, President), so I would recuse myself from the final decision on that candidate or at least declare the connection. For B031, I have long-running exchanges with the University of Tokyo and I am a Fellow there since 2025, where Katori is based; this is a general institutional link, not a personal or collaborative one, and I do not consider it a conflict. Göran Johansson is a Chalmers Physics colleague but this does not bear on the candidates I discuss.
